The social media visual and acoustic signals must contain depression-related behavioral evidence, and the datasets must represent the intended screening population well enough for the learned relations to transfer. The similarity rules used to build the graph must connect meaningful cues, not platform habits, recording quality, demographics, or other shortcuts. The abstract reports dataset experiments, but it does not prove clinical validity, fairness across groups, privacy acceptability, or safety in deployment. It also does not show from the text alone how missing modalities, noisy videos, deliberate self-presentation, or changing platform behavior affect the prediction probability.

1028.bp: This paper serves the moment when a recommender has to decide what a person is likely to click, watch, read, or buy next from an ordered history. The order matters because a recent burst of actions may show an immediate mission, while older repeated behavior may show slower taste. Frequency-domain sequential recommendation starts from a simple observation: a behavior sequence can be read not only as item after item, but also as a mixture of slow and fast changes. Slow movement may reflect stable preference; fast movement may reflect sudden interest, switching, or noise. The paper argues that current frequency-based methods are too blunt. They strengthen high-frequency parts to capture behavioral fluctuation, but this can also strengthen random noise. BFDRec is built to separate useful short-term fluctuation from useless disturbance, while also giving long-term and short-term preference their own modeling paths before combining them for next-item recommendation.
1028.wh: The hard part is that user behavior changes at more than one speed. A person may have a durable preference for science fiction, a weekly interest in headphones, and a one-click accident caused by a misplaced tap. In a sequence, all three appear as item events. A model that treats the sequence as one undivided signal has to learn slow preference and quick fluctuation through the same machinery, even though they behave differently over time. A frequency transformation, which rewrites the sequence into slower and faster components, helps expose those speeds. But the abstract says existing methods often use coarse spectrum reweighting, meaning broad frequency regions are strengthened together. That is dangerous because high-frequency bands contain both meaningful sudden changes and random noise. If the model amplifies the whole band, it may become more sensitive to accidental behavior exactly when it was trying to catch short-term intent.
1028.naive: A smart beginner might take the user's recent item sequence, transform it into frequency bands, and simply boost the fast-changing parts because next-item choice often depends on recent activity. Then the same network could process the whole transformed sequence and output item scores. This is attractive because it is compact: one transformation, one model, one ranking. It fails in two ways described by the abstract. First, fast-changing bands are not pure intent; they also contain random disturbances, so boosting them can make noise louder. Second, long-term and short-term preferences have different temporal shapes. Forcing both through one shared path can blur a stable taste with a temporary fluctuation.
1028.ap: The core idea is balanced separation. BFDRec first treats the frequency view of a user sequence as a set of bands with different energy levels. Energy here means how much signal strength appears in a band. Instead of blindly raising broad high-frequency regions, the model looks within each band and suppresses low-energy parts that are more likely to be noise, while keeping stronger fluctuation signals that may reflect real behavioral change. Then it avoids making one backbone network carry every kind of preference. It builds a multi-scale decoupled architecture: separate paths are tailored to preference patterns that unfold at different speeds. Finally, a dynamic gate combines those paths. The gate is a learned switch or mixer that decides how much each scale should matter for this user sequence before the final recommendation scores are produced.
1028.mech: The mechanism begins with an ordered list of user interactions and a catalog of candidate items to rank. First, the sequence is represented in a form the model can process, then a spectral transformation rewrites the ordered behavior into frequency components. In plain terms, the sequence is decomposed into slower waves and faster waves: slower parts stand for broad preference continuity, while faster parts stand for quick movement or sudden changes. BFDRec then examines the energy distribution inside each frequency band. Low-energy pieces are treated as likely weak disturbance and are adaptively suppressed, rather than being strengthened just because they sit in a high-frequency region. Stronger fluctuation signals are preserved because they may carry short-term intent. After this denoising step, the model sends different scale information through decoupled modeling paths. One path can specialize in slower, longer preference structure; another can specialize in quicker, shorter preference movement. The abstract does not give the internal layer equations, so the safe description is architectural: each path transforms the part of the sequence suited to its time scale into a preference signal. A dynamic gating mechanism then compares or weights these signals for the current case, producing an integrated user preference representation. That combined signal is used to score candidate items, and the output is a ranked recommendation list where higher positions are meant to match the user's next likely interaction.
1028.math: The first mathematical idea is frequency decomposition, which is a way to describe an ordered signal by how quickly it changes. The ordinary version is hearing a chord as a mixture of low and high notes. For user behavior, the low-frequency part changes slowly and can describe stable interest; the high-frequency part changes quickly and can describe short-term intent or random jumps. The second idea is energy-aware denoising. Energy is a measure of signal strength within a component. If a part of a band carries little energy, BFDRec treats it as less trustworthy and suppresses it, while preserving salient fluctuations with stronger evidence. This is a tradeoff between sensitivity and false alarm: catch quick preference changes without treating every small twitch as meaning. The third idea is decoupled multi-scale modeling. Decoupling means using separate learned transformations for patterns that live on different time scales, instead of forcing one transformation to explain all of them. The fourth idea is gating, a learned weighted mixture. Rather than hand-writing a rule such as 'recent behavior always wins,' the gate learns how much long-term and short-term signals should contribute for each sequence. The final ranking is an optimization problem in the plain sense: learn settings that put actually useful next items higher and wrong candidates lower.
1028.dots: This paper sits inside the recommender-systems family because it is about choosing a short useful list from a large catalog under partial evidence. It connects most directly to the repo's sequence concept: the ordered past is not a bag of clicks, and the system must decide which parts of that past still matter now. It also connects to similarity and ranking. After BFDRec builds an integrated preference signal, candidate items must be compared against it and sorted, so the practical outcome is still a ranked next-item list. The paper is a sibling of other sequential recommendation work in the current JSON data that separates stable preference from immediate intent, handles sparse or noisy histories, or combines different behavioral signals. Its distinctive angle is the frequency view: instead of only asking which past item is important, it asks which speed of behavioral change is important and which apparent change is just noise.
1028.ww: The reason this should improve over the naive approach is that it matches the structure of the problem more closely. User histories naturally mix slow and fast evidence. If a model is allowed to separate those speeds, it can avoid making a single internal path compromise between stable taste and immediate intent. The energy-aware step matters because high-frequency information is double-edged. Sudden changes can be exactly what the next recommendation needs, but small random fluctuations can look similar if the model only sees that they are fast. Looking at energy within each band gives the model a finer test: preserve fluctuation that has enough strength to deserve attention, and quiet weak pieces that are more likely accidental. The dynamic gate adds another layer of adaptation. Some sequences may be dominated by long-term preference; others may be dominated by a recent mission. A learned mixer can change that balance case by case. The abstract's reported improvements in hit rate and discounted ranking quality fit this intuition: better noise control and better time-scale separation should place relevant next items closer to the top.
1028.po: The payoff is a sequential recommender that is less blunt about time. According to the abstract, BFDRec suppresses noise while preserving salient behavioral fluctuations, models multi-scale user preferences, and integrates those preferences through a dynamic gate. Experiments across five real-world datasets report average improvements of 6.67% in HR and 5.05% in NDCG, which are measures of whether relevant items appear in the recommendation list and whether they appear near the top. In practical terms, the system buys more accurate next-item ranking when user histories contain both stable taste and noisy short-term movement.
1028.limits: The abstract supports the high-level mechanism but not every implementation detail, so claims about exact internal layers or training equations should not be invented. The method assumes the frequency view separates useful temporal structure from noise well enough for energy to be informative. That can fail if low-energy events are rare but important, or if strong fluctuations come from repeated accidents, bots, promotions, or exposure created by the recommender itself. The long-term and short-term paths also rely on enough historical data to learn their roles. The reported gains are across five real-world datasets, but the abstract does not prove reliability for every catalog, cold-start user, business objective, or changing deployment setting.

1029.bp: A multimodal large language model is asked to answer using both words and visual evidence. That makes its stored knowledge more than a text fact. It may include what an object looks like, what a caption means, and how the model ties the two together when answering a visual question. Over time, some of that knowledge becomes wrong or stale. A product changes, a visual fact was learned incorrectly, or a model answers a question about an image using an outdated association. The practical need is to correct that one piece without rebuilding the whole model and without damaging nearby behavior. This paper studies multimodal knowledge editing: changing wrong image-language knowledge while preserving reliability, generality, and locality. Its focus is in-context editing, where the correction is supplied at inference time through context rather than by permanently changing the model's stored weights. NeuCon-ICE asks how to make that temporary correction controlled instead of hopeful.
1029.wh: The hard part is that a multimodal model does not keep a fact in one visible drawer. A wrong answer can arise from visual processing, language processing, their interaction, or the later answer generator that combines them. In-context editing is attractive because it avoids direct surgery on the model's internal weights, so it should reduce broad side effects. But the abstract says existing in-context editing relies too much on implicit contextualization. In plain terms, the user gives corrective context and hopes the model happens to let that context influence the right internal computation at the right moment. That is out of control because the correction may be ignored, overused, or applied to cases where it should not fire. The paper identifies two missing controls: where the responsible key units are inside the model, and under what triggering conditions the correction should actually be injected.
1029.naive: A smart beginner would put the corrected fact into the prompt: here is the image-related fact you should use, now answer the question. This is simple and avoids retraining. It fails because the prompt does not say which internal part of the model should change its behavior. The model may read the new context but still follow an older image-language association, or it may apply the correction too broadly. Another beginner might directly fine-tune the model on the corrected example, but that risks changing many behaviors at once. The abstract frames NeuCon-ICE as a middle path: keep the edit at inference time, but guide it toward the internal units most tied to the multimodal context.
1029.ap: The core idea is to turn in-context editing from a whole-prompt nudge into a targeted internal intervention. NeuCon-ICE first tries to answer the where question. It identifies multimodal contextual neurons, meaning internal units whose activity appears tightly coupled to the image-language context relevant to the edit. A neuron here is just a small computational unit inside the model whose output helps shape later representations and answers. Once the likely responsible units are found, the method answers the how question. It selectively injects context-aware updates into those units, so the correction enters the model at the place where the relevant visual and textual evidence is being combined. The abstract calls this neuron-level controllable in-context editing. The important move is not simply adding more context, but using context to steer specific internal activity under defined triggering conditions.
1029.mech: The input is an editing case for a multimodal large language model: some visual-language knowledge is outdated or incorrect, and a corrective context is available at inference time. First, the model processes the image, the text, and the editing context in the ordinary forward pass. NeuCon-ICE then uses a multimodal contextual neuron identification module to look for internal units whose behavior is tightly coupled to that context. The abstract does not give the exact scoring formula, so the safe mechanical description is that the module must compare internal unit activity with the presence and relevance of the multimodal edit, then select units that look responsible for carrying the editable association. This produces a target set: where the edit should enter. Second, the context-aware neuron editing module decides how to alter those selected units. Instead of rewriting all model settings or trusting the prompt alone, it injects an update into the chosen units when the triggering conditions indicate that the edit is relevant. The model then continues its computation with those adjusted internal signals. The output is the model's answer after the correction has been applied. The intended behavior is local: answers requiring the corrected knowledge should change, while unrelated visual-language abilities should remain stable.
1029.math: The mathematical problem is controlled influence. The model contains many internal units, and the edit should affect only a small useful subset. That creates a selection problem: among thousands or millions of possible units, choose the ones whose activity is most tied to the current multimodal context. Selection here means assigning evidence to units and keeping the highest-responsibility ones. It is a form of attribution, which in plain language asks which internal pieces helped produce the behavior we want to change. The next idea is conditional updating. A correction should not be a permanent blanket rule; it should fire when the current image-text situation matches the edit. That is a gating problem: decide when a signal is allowed through and how strongly it should influence later computation. The update itself is a small transformation of selected unit activations, not a full retraining pass according to the abstract's inference-time framing. The tradeoff is locality versus generality. If the selected unit set is too narrow, the corrected knowledge may not carry to equivalent questions. If it is too broad, unrelated answers may be disturbed. NeuCon-ICE uses neuron identification and context-aware injection as mathematical handles on that tradeoff.
1029.dots: This paper belongs to the repo's LLMs and language-models family because it adds control around a fluent but unreliable model: the issue is not whether the model can answer, but whether its answer uses corrected knowledge in the right circumstances. It also sits in the multimodal vision-language family, where different channels must be aligned without erasing what each channel contributes. Neighboring retrieval and question-answering papers worry about choosing the right outside evidence before a model speaks; NeuCon-ICE worries about where that evidence should enter inside the model. It also connects to attention as selective influence, although here the selection is over internal neurons rather than document passages or image regions. The shared conference pressure is controllability. Modern systems are too large to fix by hand and too useful to discard when one fact is wrong, so many papers ask how to change a specific behavior while protecting the rest.
1029.ww: The approach should work better than naive prompting because it reduces the gap between supplying a correction and making the model actually use it. A prompt-level edit depends on the model's ordinary context handling, which may or may not route the correction to the computation that produced the wrong multimodal answer. By first identifying responsible multimodal contextual neurons, NeuCon-ICE gives the correction a more precise entry point. If those units truly carry the image-language association being edited, changing their activity should alter the answer more directly than adding more words to the context. The context-aware trigger matters because knowledge editing is not only about changing one answer; it is about changing it under the right conditions. A correction about one visual fact should generalize to close paraphrases or related visual questions, but it should not leak into unrelated cases. Selective injection can therefore support reliability, generality, and locality at the same time: reliability by making the edit active, generality by tying it to context rather than a single wording, and locality by limiting where the model is touched.
1029.po: The payoff is a more controllable way to correct multimodal models at inference time. The abstract says NeuCon-ICE is evaluated on three representative MLLMs: BLIP-2, MiniGPT-4, and LLaVA 1.5, with ComprehendEdit and an E-VQA demo named in the provided text. Grounded in that evidence, the claimed capability is not a new general model, but a targeted editing procedure: locate responsible multimodal contextual neurons and inject context-aware updates into them. Practically, that buys a way to repair stale or incorrect visual-language knowledge while aiming to preserve reliability, generality, and locality.
1029.limits: The provided abstract is truncated after the benchmark names, so it does not show the full experimental results, metrics, or failure cases. The method assumes that responsible multimodal knowledge can be localized to identifiable contextual neurons and that editing their activity is enough to change the answer without hidden side effects elsewhere. That may fail when a fact is spread across many units, when the trigger is ambiguous, or when image and text cues conflict. It also assumes the identification module can distinguish true responsibility from correlation. The abstract supports tests on three model families, but not universal reliability across all multimodal models, domains, or adversarial prompts.

1030.bp: When you see the name 'Washington' in text, does it mean the US state, the capital city, or a person's surname? The answer depends on context and corroborating signals. Multimodal entity linking uses text, images, and structured knowledge together to disambiguate. The challenge is that different modalities offer contradictory clues, and one modality can dominate unfairly, drowning out the others. A fair system balances all signals.
1030.wh: Existing systems either couple all modalities tightly (so one error propagates to all) or use global aggregation (averaging modality signals, which loses nuance). Some entities have clear visual signatures (the Statue of Liberty is distinctive), while others are only identified by text or metadata. Forcing a uniform strategy ignores these differences. The system also needs to know not just if the modalities agree, but precisely how they should agree.
1030.ap: This paper uses expert networks that handle different aspects of the problem in parallel (a divide-and-conquer strategy). Each expert specializes in one type of correspondence—say, visual cues or textual mention patterns. The system learns which experts should matter using a routing mechanism guided by KL divergence (a measure of how different two probability distributions are). It also builds a hierarchical graph showing relationships at multiple levels of detail, and lets the modalities refine each other through this graph rather than just averaging.
1030.ww: By separating the problem into independent experts, one modality's error does not ruin the others. The KL-guided routing means experts learn to specialize: one might focus on visual cues, another on mention patterns, and the system adaptively weights their input. The hierarchical graph captures both coarse (this is a person, not a place) and fine (this is a historical figure, not a celebrity) distinctions.
1030.po: On benchmark datasets for multimodal entity linking, the system consistently ranks higher than prior methods, correctly disambiguating entity mentions even when modalities conflict. The improvements are largest on ambiguous cases where modalities gave contradictory signals.

1031.bp: Complex questions often need multi-step reasoning: 'Which Nobel Prize winners published papers at MIT in the last five years?' requires finding Nobel laureates, checking their MIT affiliations, and verifying recent publications. Typical retrieval-augmented generation systems treat this as one big retrieval problem, but the reasoning and retrieval needed for each step is different. Splitting the task into specialized subtasks could work better.
1031.wh: A single model trying to handle high-level planning (what are the sub-questions?) and detailed execution (find papers on this specific topic) ends up doing both poorly. It gets distracted by irrelevant details while trying to plan, or loses sight of the big picture while executing. Also, different parts of the question benefit from different tools—some need a fact-checking database, others need semantic search.
1031.ap: This paper separates the task into two layers. A high-level planner decomposes the complex question into subtasks and coordinates the overall strategy. For each subtask, a specialized agent equipped with specific tools (knowledge bases, search engines, reasoning modules) handles execution. The planner reasons about how to combine the results from different agents into a final answer. Each agent can focus on its own domain without distraction from the overall goal.
1031.ww: By separating planning from execution, the planner can think strategically without the noise of implementation details. Each specialized agent becomes expert in its domain because it sees only relevant subtasks. This mirrors how humans solve complex problems—we break them down, assign specialists to pieces, then synthesize results—rather than trying to do everything with one person.
1031.po: On complex cross-modal search benchmarks (questions that require combining information from text, tables, and images), this hierarchical approach significantly outperforms flat retrieval-augmented generation systems. The separation of concerns leads to both better reasoning and better execution.

1032.bp: When an AI agent needs to retrieve a table from a database to answer a user's instruction—'find a table with sales data by quarter, excluding 2024'—relevance depends on both topical similarity (sales, quarterly) and following specific constraints (exclude a year, include certain columns). Existing table retrieval systems focus on topical relevance alone and ignore constraints. A system needs to actually follow instructions.
1032.wh: Topical relevance and instruction-following are fundamentally different tasks. A table about 'quarterly sales for all years' is topically relevant but disobeys the 'exclude 2024' instruction. Existing systems have no way to model constraint satisfaction separately from semantic similarity. Also, schema awareness is weak: most systems do not reason carefully about column names and data representation choices.
1032.ap: This paper formalizes a new task: instruction-following table retrieval, where a system must find tables that satisfy both topical relevance and explicit constraints. It introduces a benchmark with tables annotated for inclusion/exclusion requirements and schema constraints. It also proposes a new metric that checks whether retrieval rankings actually adapt to the instruction (compared to ignoring the instruction). The benchmark is large-scale and created via a structured annotation pipeline.
1032.ww: By making constraint satisfaction a formal requirement and measuring it separately, systems can now be trained and evaluated on following instructions. The metric catches systems that do well on topical retrieval but ignore constraints. Schema awareness naturally improves because the benchmark explicitly rewards understanding column semantics and representation choices.
1032.po: The benchmark reveals that existing retrieval models struggle with fine-grained instruction constraints, exhibiting systematic biases toward surface-level semantic cues. By providing the first large-scale evaluation setting for instruction-following table retrieval, it enables future research in this underexplored area and reveals current systems' blind spots.

1033.bp: Generative recommendation systems create a personalized ranking by generating predictions directly, rather than computing similarity scores. Flow matching (a deep generative technique) has been applied here with promise. Yet the standard training objective does not push different users toward different preferences. Without explicit separation between users, the system generates bland, averaged preferences that do not distinguish one person from another.
1033.wh: Directly applying contrastive learning (a technique that pushes different entities apart) to the final output of a flow model causes false repulsion: if two users happen to like the same movie, pushing their scores apart makes the model learn something false. Flow matching is also sensitive to input perturbations, so standard contrastive learning view construction breaks the output—positive pairs become semantically mismatched.
1033.ap: Instead of contrasting the final predictions, this paper applies contrastive learning inside the model, at an intermediate layer (the encoder) before the final output. This avoids the false repulsion problem: even if two users have similar final preferences, their internal representations can still be pushed apart. The system decomposes the flow model into an encoder (shared across users) and a prediction head (per-user), applying contrastive regularization to the encoder representations.
1033.ww: Constraining users' internal representations to be distinct does not force their final preferences to be different. This solves the false repulsion problem: the model learns to represent users differently internally, which naturally leads to personalized outputs without breaking semantic meaning. The encoder-head decomposition provides a clean place to apply the constraint without disrupting the flow-matching process.
1033.po: On collaborative filtering benchmarks, the contrastive flow matching approach generates more diverse and personalized recommendations compared to flow matching with only regression loss. User separation leads to higher-quality rankings where individual preferences come through, not averaged preferences.

1034.bp: LLM-based agents can do complex tasks by calling external tools. But which tool to use? If the tool descriptions are vague ('format: string', 'does conversion'), the agent wastes time trying wrong tools or gives up. This is an acute problem for the Model Context Protocol ecosystem, where thousands of third-party tools exist and descriptions are often unclear. Automating the generation of clear, function-oriented documentation could solve this.
1034.wh: Tool creators write documentation in free-form text, emphasizing human readability over machine searchability. They often hide the actual function signatures inside code, leaving them out of docs entirely. When tools have overlapping names or ambiguous descriptions, an LLM agent retrieving tools sees only noise. The gap between implementation and documentation makes retrieval nearly impossible.
1034.ap: This paper builds an automated pipeline that extracts the actual tool implementation from source code (a white-box analysis), generates precise descriptions for each function based on what the code does, then aggregates these into a structured server-level overview. The pipeline operates in stages: extract tool inventory with metadata, refine each tool's description grounded in its implementation, synthesize a searchable server overview. It also constructs a benchmark of real-world tool discovery queries to measure retrieval quality.
1034.ww: By grounding descriptions in the actual code implementation, there is no gap between documentation and reality. The staged approach (tool-level then server-level) means detailed function information is preserved and then intelligently summarized. The benchmark enables evaluation of retrieval quality, showing whether descriptions are actually useful for finding tools.
1034.po: On a benchmark of 3000+ real open-source MCP servers, the system generates structured documentation that significantly improves tool discovery retrieval compared to raw, unstructured documentation. Agents can now find the right tools more reliably, making complex multi-step tool workflows more practical.
